title: Fats & Oils
subtitle: 1500–1750 · Whale Oil Goes Industrial: Basques at Red Bay, the Dutch at Spitsbergen, Luther’s Butter, Palm Oil in the Slave Ship and the Ming Oil Press

entries.label: English and Dutch whalers fight over Spitsbergen
entries.hint: After James I chartered the Muscovy Company to fish Spitsbergen, the Dutch answered in 1614 with their own Noordsche Compagnie. In 1613 four Dutch and twelve Spanish ships were chased off by the English, who had armed their whalers; by 1615 whale ships and warships of the two nations stood in conflict in the fjords, and both saw that whaling as an adjunct to naval war would ruin them. The quarrel resurfaced in 1651, when England’s Navigation Act was meant to restrict Dutch whale oil, which undercut English prices, and a Dutch war followed, ending in 1654.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly summary): Ellis, Men and Whales (1991) pp.47, 57 and 60 (PDF pp.70, 80, 83). The war of 1652–54 had many causes; Ellis’s link to whale oil is one of them and should not be read as the cause.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: Elizabeth’s whaling monopoly, soap-oil fines, whale-oil duties and colonial drift-whale rules

entries.label: Elizabeth I grants a whaling monopoly “within any seas whatsoever”
entries.hint: In 1576 Queen Elizabeth awarded the Muscovy Company, which traded cloth and firearms to Russia for fish, oil and timber, a twenty-year monopoly to hunt whales ‘within any seas whatsoever’. The English were not particularly successful; the Basques they hired as harpooners were the only people, in the captain Jonas Poole’s words, who ‘understood whaling’.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly summary): Ellis (1991) pp.50–51 and 53 (PDF pp.73–74, 76). The identification of the 1576 grantee as the Muscovy Company follows Ellis’s narrative of the company that grew from the Merchant Adventurers.

entries.label: London fines soap-makers who use anything but pure olive oil
entries.hint: In 1618 London authorities fined, and jailed, soap-makers who used any oil but pure olive oil — an early attempt to police what went into a fat product, in a trade where adulteration with cheaper oils was a long-running problem. Two decades later an agent in Livorno blamed worms in English cloth on clothiers who, since the planting of rapeseed in England, had learned to mix that oil with olive oil.
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular history; the 1618 order not read): Mueller, Extra Virginity (2011), the passage on adulteration in the Venetian oil trade, citing a letter of the Livorno agent of Fairfax and Barnsley. Whether the rule was enforced is not shown.

entries.label: Colonies regulate drift whales: Massachusetts 1641, Southampton 1644
entries.hint: Colonial towns began to regulate the whales cast up on their shores. In 1641 the Massachusetts Bay General Court ordered that any whale cast up be kept or ‘improved’ (boiled for oil) by the town or owner until it set order; in 1644 the Southampton court on Long Island divided the town into four wards of eleven persons who cut up whales by lot, with a double share of blubber for the cutters, watchmen after storms and a five-shilling finder’s fee.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Dolin, Leviathan: The History of Whaling in America (2007; 2016 ed.) ch.3, pp.82–83 (PDF pp.82–83; Winthrop’s journal of 1635 for the first oil from a Cape Cod whale; the Massachusetts order of 1641; Southampton’s court of 7 March 1644).

entries.label: England protects its whale oil: the Navigation Act and the 1672 duties
entries.hint: England’s Navigation Act of 1651 aimed to restrict the sale of Dutch whale oil in England. An Act of 1672 removed all duties on whale products brought in by Englishmen, while foreigners paid £9 a ton on oil and twice as much on bone; a Company of Merchants Trading with Greenland was capitalised at £40,000 in 1693.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly summary): Ellis (1991) pp.60 and 68 (PDF pp.83, 91). Ellis dates the Dutch price advantage to their more efficient fishery.

entries.label: Luther rails at the Lenten oil and the sale of butter
entries.hint: In 1520 Luther wrote that in Rome they mock fasting, forcing northerners to eat an oil they would not use to grease their shoes, then sell the right to eat forbidden foods; eating butter, they say, is a greater sin than to lie or blaspheme. Flandrin argues that northern Europe’s repugnance for cooking in oil helped throw it into the Reformation; Khosrova notes that the dairy-rich countries were largely the nations that broke from Rome in the sixteenth century.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Khosrova, Butter (2016) pp.56–57 (PDF pp.77–78), quoting Luther as cited in Henisch, Fast and Feast; Flandrin, L’ordre des mets, on Lent and the Reformation (the claim is his hypothesis, not established); compare fats-1000-1500::o2 for the butter dispensations that Luther attacks.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Carnival against Lent; the candles of Versailles

entries.label: The war of Carnival and Lent: butter against olive oil
entries.hint: From the fifteenth century on, the struggle between oil and butter was staged in paintings, literature and street dramas as the war between Carnival and Lent, with butter marching in full armour at the head of animal fats and dairy foods, and olive oil leading herrings, cabbage, bread and other Lenten allies. The span follows Mueller’s ‘from the fifteenth century down through the nineteenth’.
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular history; works not named): Mueller (2011), the passage on the culinary divide of north and south.

entries.label: Twenty-four thousand lights for the park of Versailles
entries.hint: In 1688 some 24,000 lights were burnt to illuminate the park of Versailles alone — presumably all wax candles, an extremely costly form of lighting normally reserved for royal displays. The light of fats was a sign of wealth. Schivelbusch describes the traditional pre-industrial lights as candles and oil lamps.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly book read): Schivelbusch, Disenchanted Night (1988) ch.1 (PDF p.10) — ‘in 1688, 24,000 lights were used to illuminate the park of Versailles alone, presumably all wax candles’. The tallow and oil-lamp remark is the folio’s context, with Schivelbusch’s description of the pre-industrial candle and lamp.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Butter and leprosy; the sunflower; the Tiangong kaiwu’s oil ranking

entries.label: The Cardinal of Aragon: butter countries are overrun with lepers
entries.hint: The Cardinal of Aragon, travelling through the Low Countries in 1517 with his own cook and a large supply of olive oil, observed warily that, because of the butter and dairy produce so widely used in Flanders and Germany, these countries were ‘overrun with lepers’. The Gonzaga of Mantua likewise took ‘good oil’ with them to England; southern Europeans regarded butter as unnatural and unhealthy.
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular history): Mueller (2011), the passage on the culinary divide of north and south. The belief that butter caused leprosy is also in fats-1000-1500::b1 (Khosrova on Provençal and Spanish travellers).

entries.label: The sunflower reaches Europe
entries.hint: The sunflower, domesticated in eastern North America, was carried to Europe after 1492, probably first to Spain, where it was taken in 1569 as an ornamental. The first clear reference is Rembert Dodoens’s herbal of 1568, where it is illustrated, and it reached England before the end of the century. It would be grown for oil mainly in Russia.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Kiple, Cambridge World History of Food (2000) II.E.1 p.382 (PDF p.419, ‘taken to Spain in 1569’) and II.E.6 p.428 (PDF p.465, the Dodoens reference). The 1568/1569 dates differ in the two chapters of the same work.

entries.label: Song Yingxing ranks the oils: what to eat, what to burn
entries.hint: In the Tiangong kaiwu (1637) Song Yingxing ranks oils by use. For eating the best are those of sesame, turnip seed, yellow soybean and cabbage seed, then perilla and rapeseed, then tea seed, and last hemp seed. For lamps the best is tallow-tree kernel oil, then rapeseed, linseed, cottonseed and sesame (which burns off too quickly), with tung oil and mixed tallow-seed oil worst. Castor and perilla oils are prepared by boiling, not pressing.
entries.note: SECONDARY (translation read in Needham): Needham, SCC 6.5 (2000) pp.450–452 (PDF pp.478–480), citing TKKW ch.12 pp.209–211 in the translation of Sun & Sun (1966). The yields in catties per tan are in the table at p.451–452.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: Red Bay, Spitsbergen, Leith soap-boilers, the Mortamer ledger, Dutch butter, colonial sesame

entries.label: Butter becomes a status symbol in Italy
entries.hint: In Italy the medieval peasant could rarely afford good olive oil, and lard was forbidden on fast days, leaving them cheap, foul-tasting oil. When the Church allowed butter in Lent in the north, the practice spread south, and by the sixteenth century butter had become a status symbol, above all among the nobility of the southern cities: the difficulty of getting and keeping it in a hot climate made it more desirable as a luxury.
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular history, citing Capatti): Khosrova (2016) p.57 (PDF p.78), citing Alberto Capatti’s Italian Cuisine: A Cultural History. Capatti was not read.

entries.label: Red Bay, Labrador: the Basques’ whale-oil station
entries.hint: At Red Bay in Labrador, where the Basques colonised about 1540, the first whaling station in North America has been found, dating from about 1536: the wreck of a three-masted galleon thought to have sunk in a storm in 1565, a chalupa hull, and tryworks on the smaller islands where blubber was rendered to oil, in use in 1560–1570. The legend that the Basques invented shipboard tryworks seems apocryphal. After the Armada of 1588 Spain could no longer protect the distant fleets and the fishery declined.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly summary): Ellis, Men and Whales (1991) pp.46–48 and 53 (PDF pp.69–71, 76), citing Barkham’s archival work in Spain. Aguilar estimates the Basque catch for 1530–1610; the figure is not reproduced here.

entries.label: The Dutch ‘butterboxes’ of the Golden Age
entries.hint: Holland became the foremost maritime and dairy-producing power of the 1600s partly because Dutch farmers built grazing soil from manure, street sweepings, bird droppings and commercial waste, including ash from soap making. An English diplomat, William Aglionby, wrote that Dutch cows gave ‘great store of milk, of which is made excellent butter’; the envious English called the Dutch ‘butterboxes’.
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular history): Khosrova (2016) p.21 (PDF p.42), quoting Aglionby. The reading of the English nickname is Khosrova’s.

entries.label: The Dutch build a whale-oil industry at Spitsbergen
entries.hint: In 1611 Muscovy Company ships under Thomas Edge reached Spitsbergen with six Basque harpooners from St-Jean-de-Luz, one of whom killed the first whale there; blubber was stripped, boiled in shore furnaces and the oil run into casks. The Dutch founded Smeerenburg about 1620, and their fleet grew from 30–40 ships in 1642 to 178 by 1670. The last Dutch land station at Spitsbergen closed in 1670.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly summary): Ellis (1991) pp.47, 53–57, 64–65 (PDF pp.70, 76–80, 87–88), citing Hakluyt, Conway’s History of Spitsbergen and Hacquebord for the tryworks of about 1615. A warm spell from 1625 to 1635 moved the whales offshore (see w1).

entries.label: Palm oil crosses to Brazil: the 1642 ledger of Pieter Mortamer
entries.hint: A 1642 ledger of the Dutch merchant Pieter Mortamer records a continuing exchange of palm oil and kernels moving from Angola and the island of São Tomé to Brazil. Palm oil was among the staples of the West African ports the Portuguese and others visited, and the oil palm groves coincide almost exactly with the regions from which the enslaved were embarked.
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular history; ledger not read): Zuckerman, Planet Palm (2021) ch.1 (‘the 1642 ledger of a Dutch merchant named Pieter Mortamer’), citing the map of oil-palm groves and embarkation regions; Lynn, Commerce and Economic Change in West Africa (1997) Introduction p.2 (the first recorded English purchase, 1588, by Captain Walsh at Benin).

entries.label: Sesame as a British colonial hope, and as the African ‘benne’
entries.hint: The British hoped sesame grown in their American colonies might replace the olive oil they bought from European rivals, so that sesame became one of the commodities whose colonial production they encouraged. The seed may in fact have come with Africans: in the southern United States one of its names is benne, from Bambara and Wolof bene. Nineteenth-century France, in contrast, forbade sesame to protect its rapeseed growers.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly chapter): Kiple (2000) II.E.4 p.418 (PDF p.455), citing Wilson 1964 and Turner 1969 (Africanisms in Gullah); Jessica Harris’s comment is a personal communication. The date range is the folio’s for the colonial period; Kiple does not date the British encouragement.

entries.label: Soap-boilers of Leith put money into a whaling voyage
entries.hint: In the season of 1682–83 a company of merchants and soap-boilers from Leith invested £1,700 in a whaling voyage that returned a profit of £525 — a sign of the whale oil’s role as raw material for soap and lighting, and of the way the whale fishery was financed by the trades that used its oil.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly summary): Ellis (1991) p.61 (PDF p.84). Ellis gives no further detail of the voyage; the link to soap is the investors’ trade.

entries.label: London’s tallow chandlers cannot make enough candles
entries.hint: In 1694–95 the apothecary and grocer John Houghton estimated that London-based tallow production was about 5 million pounds of fat a year and noted it was not sufficient. Rendering fat was a task of the tallow-chandler, whose trade was tied to candle-making; butchers took blocks of visceral fat as part of their pay, and the senior kitchen staff of a household kept the ‘kitchen-stuff’. Houghton wrote articles on tallow, tallow candles and soap, and described soap-makers’ and chandlers’ trades.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly essay read): Lowengard, ‘On the Disappearance of the Animal Body’, Historical Studies in the Natural Sciences 53(3) (2023) pp.242–244, citing Houghton’s Collection for the Improvement of Husbandry and Trade (1694/5). Houghton’s figure is a contemporary estimate, quoted by Lowengard without checking.

entries.label: The Ming wedge press: roast, roll, steam, press twice
entries.hint: The Tiangong kaiwu describes the Chinese oil press as a hollowed log of camphorwood, sandalwood or alder, with steamed seed cakes wrapped in straw packed in the trough and a wedge driven in by a battering ram; seed is roasted, rolled in a mill (an ox does the work of ten men) and steamed, quick wrapping being ‘the secret’ of yield. Pressed cakes are re-ground and pressed a second time for half as much oil. Needham finds this practically identical to Wang Zhen’s press of 1313 and to Chhi min yao shu practice.
entries.note: SECONDARY (translation read in Needham): Needham, SCC 6.5 (2000) pp.444–450 (PDF pp.472–478) with Figs 98–103; also p.452 on the Indian ghani, said to have been in use continuously from the 7th century BC, and the Japanese press of 1836. The 1637 date is that of the Tiangong kaiwu; the press it describes is older.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Olive oil and olive trees to the Americas

entries.label: Olive oil to the Americas, then the olive itself
entries.hint: After the conquest, American demand stimulated Spain’s olive oil industry; as the colonists began making their own oil the flow across the Atlantic diminished. Religious orders planted olives in their settlements all over South America, and as the missionaries moved north, so did the trees — oil being an ingredient of chrism and so a vehicle of conversion.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Kiple (2000) II.E.1 p.378 (PDF p.415; Spain’s industry stimulated by American demand) and Mueller (2011), the chapter on the New World (religious orders planting olives; Serra in 1769 is in fats-1750-1850). Neither gives dates for the missions’ planting.

entries.label: A warm decade moves the whales offshore
entries.hint: Pollen studies identify a warm period from 1625 to 1635; as the Gulf Stream moved farther from Norway and the edge of the pack ice withdrew from Spitsbergen, the whales stayed farther offshore, making the bay whaling of the shore stations harder — one background to the shift from shore tryworks to ships that rendered at sea.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly summary): Ellis (1991) p.64 (PDF p.87), citing pollen studies. The link to the shift from shore stations to ships is the folio’s inference; the last Dutch shore station closed in 1670 (see ec2).

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: Palm oil on the slave ships

entries.label: Palm oil in the slave ship’s pot
entries.hint: On the slave ships crossing the Atlantic, women captives were often charged with pounding and boiling palm fruits to make the oil that seasoned the gruel fed to the others; a British seizure of a Spanish schooner in 1838 listed ‘three cauldrons for clarifying palm-oil’ among the signs it had very recently landed a cargo of slaves. As ships neared port the oil was rubbed into captives’ skin to hide wounds and scars and make them look more attractive to buyers.
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular history; sources not read): Zuckerman, Planet Palm (2021) ch.1; Lynn (1997) Introduction p.2 on palm oil used for provisions on the voyage to the Americas. The 1838 seizure is quoted by Zuckerman. The practice is attested for the whole period of the trade, so the date is a span.
